steps.text:
## Introduction

Neural oscillations and the spatial organization of neural activity have been of great interest in the neuroscience community ever since the earliest neural recordings. Because of this, the literature has put forward a lot of hypothesized functions for these widely observed phenomena. For example: one proposal is that alpha oscillations do 'cortical scanning' like radar; another suggests that synchrony may segregate the visual scene and 'bind' individual features into cohesive objects; others suggest brain-wide oscillations act as 'top-down' stored knowledge and contextual influence for local processing; another study shows theta is consistent with a gating mechanism for human working memory; some posit that oscillations form a hierarchical system that gives a syntactical structure for spike traffic; and two further studies connect oscillatory coherence with the transfer of information on working memory tasks.

Recently, high density multi-electrode arrays and high resolution imaging have led to the discovery that many oscillations in the brain are better described as traveling waves of activity and not precise zero-lag synchrony. For example, alpha and theta oscillations were measured to correspond precisely to traveling waves in both the cortex and hippocampus of humans. It has also become more and more clear that wave-like dynamics are prevalent throughout the brain, from local to global scales, and across virtually all brain regions measured. Research has correlated wave activity with many functional roles, about as diverse and numerous as for oscillations, including: perceptual awareness; attentional scanning; information transfer; motor control sequencing and topographic organization; integrating visual sensory signals with saccadic eye movements; and coordinating and reconfiguring distinct functional regions.

Most relevant for this study, a lot of work has shown correlations between wave dynamics and memory. For example: one study gives evidence that traveling waves going from posterior to anterior cortex encode sequential stimuli in an overlapping 'multiplexed' manner; another shows that traveling theta oscillations go from anterior to posterior regions during retrieval from long-term memory; and another shows traveling beta waves in frontal and parietal lobes encode memory of recent rewards. As described in prior work, one way to understand the relation between traveling waves and memory is an analogy to physical wave systems. Specifically, it can be shown that non-dissipative wave-propagating systems contain all information about past disturbances in a 'time-reversible' manner. But in a static wave-free 'bump' system, the onset time of stimuli is tied to position, so information about the sequential order of multiple inputs at the same position is lost. This is shown in Figure 1 and demonstrated experimentally in Section 3. It is an imperfect analogy to the brain, but such ideas have inspired neuroscientists to suggest that the cortical surface may act like a wave-propagating system to efficiently encode recent sequential inputs as a form of working memory. In this work we propose a complimentary mechanistic understanding of the relation between traveling waves and memory. We suggest that a wave-propagating hidden state can be thought of like a register or 'stack' that inputs are sequentially written or 'pushed' to. The propagation of waves then stops past input from being overwritten, which allows for superior invertible memory storage.

- Traveling waves and memory
  - posterior-to-anterior waves encode sequential stimuli, 'multiplexed'
  - traveling theta, anterior to posterior, during retrieval from long-term memory
  - traveling beta waves in frontal and parietal lobes encode memory of recent rewards
  - analogy to physical wave systems: non-dissipative wave systems keep all info about past disturbances, 'time-reversible'
  - static wave-free 'bump' system: onset time tied to position -> order of inputs at same position lost (Figure 1, Section 3)
  - imperfect analogy, but cortex as wave system encoding recent sequential inputs = working memory
  - ours: wave-propagating hidden state like register / 'stack', inputs 'pushed'; propagation prevents overwriting -> invertible memory
- Controversy
  - many argue waves 'epiphenominal', inert byproduct, no causal power
  - lack of capable models to study computational role of waves on tasks
  - large-scale SNN models with traveling waves, but too complex to train on real tasks -> can't show implications for memory
  - Neural Wave Machine (ML): waves in hidden state for sequence modeling, but coupled oscillators -> can't separate oscillation vs wave contributions to memory
- Our work
  - simple non-oscillatory RNN with traveling waves in hidden state; compare with identical wave-free 'bump system' RNNs
  - wave models: longer sequence tasks, learn faster, lower error; approach more complicated SOTA architectures
  - early computational evidence for wave-based memory
  - proof of concept + starting point for future development

steps.text:
## Introduction

Neural oscillations and the spatial organization of neural activity have been of great interest in the neuroscience community ever since the earliest neural recordings. Because of this, the literature has put forward a lot of hypothesized functions for these widely observed phenomena. For example: one proposal is that alpha oscillations do 'cortical scanning' like radar; another suggests that synchrony may segregate the visual scene and 'bind' individual features into cohesive objects; others suggest brain-wide oscillations act as 'top-down' stored knowledge and contextual influence for local processing; another study shows theta is consistent with a gating mechanism for human working memory; some posit that oscillations form a hierarchical system that gives a syntactical structure for spike traffic; and two further studies connect oscillatory coherence with the transfer of information on working memory tasks.

Recently, high density multi-electrode arrays and high resolution imaging have led to the discovery that many oscillations in the brain are better described as traveling waves of activity and not precise zero-lag synchrony. For example, alpha and theta oscillations were measured to correspond precisely to traveling waves in both the cortex and hippocampus of humans. It has also become more and more clear that wave-like dynamics are prevalent throughout the brain, from local to global scales, and across virtually all brain regions measured. Research has correlated wave activity with many functional roles, about as diverse and numerous as for oscillations, including: perceptual awareness; attentional scanning; information transfer; motor control sequencing and topographic organization; integrating visual sensory signals with saccadic eye movements; and coordinating and reconfiguring distinct functional regions.

Most relevant for this study, a lot of work has shown correlations between wave dynamics and memory. For example: one study gives evidence that traveling waves going from posterior to anterior cortex encode sequential stimuli in an overlapping 'multiplexed' manner; another shows that traveling theta oscillations go from anterior to posterior regions during retrieval from long-term memory; and another shows traveling beta waves in frontal and parietal lobes encode memory of recent rewards. As described in prior work, one way to understand the relation between traveling waves and memory is an analogy to physical wave systems. Specifically, it can be shown that non-dissipative wave-propagating systems contain all information about past disturbances in a 'time-reversible' manner. But in a static wave-free 'bump' system, the onset time of stimuli is tied to position, so information about the sequential order of multiple inputs at the same position is lost. This is shown in Figure 1 and demonstrated experimentally in Section 3. It is an imperfect analogy to the brain, but such ideas have inspired neuroscientists to suggest that the cortical surface may act like a wave-propagating system to efficiently encode recent sequential inputs as a form of working memory. In this work we propose a complimentary mechanistic understanding of the relation between traveling waves and memory. We suggest that a wave-propagating hidden state can be thought of like a register or 'stack' that inputs are sequentially written or 'pushed' to. The propagation of waves then stops past input from being overwritten, which allows for superior invertible memory storage.

Along with these theories of potential function, almost as many arguments have been put forward that traveling waves are 'epiphenominal', or just the inert byproduct of more fundamental causal neural processes without any causal power of their own. One reason this controversy continues is that there are not sufficiently capable models that allow studying the computational role of waves in a task-relevant way. In the computational neuroscience literature there are large-scale spiking neural network (SNN) models which show traveling waves of activity; but because SNNs are computationally complex, it is still not feasible to train such models on real world tasks. So these models cannot demonstrate the implications of traveling waves on memory. In the machine learning community, the recently introduced Neural Wave Machine shows traveling waves of activity in its hidden state in the service of sequence modeling; but since it is built as a network of coupled oscillators, it is impossible to separate the memory-enhancing contributions of oscillations (as described in other work) from those of traveling waves.

In this work we derive and introduce a simple non-oscillatory recurrent neural network (RNN) architecture which shows traveling waves in its hidden state. We then study the performance implications of these waves, comparing directly with identical wave-free 'bump system' RNN counterparts. We find that wave-based models can solve sequence modeling tasks of significantly greater length, learn faster, and reach lower error than non-wave counterparts, and they approach the performance of more complicated state of the art architectures. This gives some of the first computational evidence for the benefits of wave-based memory systems. So we present our model both as a proof of concept of the computational role of wave-based memory systems and as a starting point for developing such systems further in the future.

Consequently, a plethora of hypothesized functions for these widely observed phenomena have been put forth in the literature. For example: [3] propose that alpha oscillations perform 'cortical scanning' akin to radar; [4] suggests that synchrony may serve to segregate the visual scene and 'bind' individual features into cohesive objects; [5] suggest brain-wide oscillations serve as 'top-down' stored knowledge and contextual influence for local processing; [6] show theta is consistent with a gating mechanism for human working memory; [7] posit that oscillations form a hierarchical system that offers a syntactical structure for spike traffic; and [8] & [9] implicate oscillatory coherence with the transfer of information on working memory tasks.

Recently, the advent of high density multi-electrode arrays and high resolution imaging has led to the discovery that many of the oscillations observed in the brain are better described as traveling waves of activity rather than precise zero-lag synchrony [10]. For example, alpha and theta oscillations have been measured to correspond precisely to traveling waves in both the cortex and hippocampus of humans [11,12,13]. Furthermore, it has become increasingly clear that wave-like dynamics are prevalent throughout the brain, from local [14] to global [15] scales, and across virtually all brain regions measured [16,17,18]. Research has correlated wave activity with a range of functional roles rivaling oscillations in diversity and number, including: perceptual awareness [19]; attentional scanning [20]; information transfer [21]; motor control sequencing and topographic organization [22]; integrating visual sensory signals with saccadic eye movements [23]; and coordinating and reconfiguring distinct functional regions [24].

Most relevant to the present study, significant work has shown correlations between wave dynamics and memory. For example: [25] provide evidence that traveling waves propagating from posterior to anterior cortex encode sequential stimuli in an overlapping 'multiplexed' manner; [26] show that traveling theta oscillations propagate from anterior to posterior regions during retrieval from long-term memory; and [27] show traveling beta waves in frontal and parietal lobes encode memory of recent rewards. As described by [10], one way to understand the relation between traveling waves and memory comes from an analogy to physical wave systems. Specifically, non-dissipative wave-propagating systems can be shown to contain all information about past disturbances in a 'time-reversible' manner. In contrast, in a static wave-free 'bump' system, the onset time of stimuli is tied to position, and therefore information about the sequential order of multiple inputs at the same position is lost. This is visualized in Figure 1 and demonstrated experimentally in Section 3. Although an imperfect analogy to the brain, such ideas have inspired neuroscientists to suggest that the cortical surface may act like such a wave-propagating system to efficiently encode recent sequential inputs as a form of working memory. In this work, we propose a complimentary mechanistic understanding of the relation between traveling waves and memory by suggesting that a wave-propagating hidden state can be thought of like a register or 'stack' to which inputs are sequentially written or 'pushed'. The propagation of waves then prevents overwriting of past input, allowing for superior invertible memory storage.

Alongside these theories of potential function, an almost equal number of arguments have been put forth suggesting that traveling waves are 'epiphenominal', or merely the inert byproduct of more fundamental causal neural processes without any causal power of their own. One factor behind the continuation of this controversy is a lack of sufficiently capable models which permit the study of the computational role of waves in a task-relevant manner. In the computational neuroscience literature, there exist large-scale spiking neural network (SNN) models which exhibit traveling waves of activity [28]; however, due to the computational complexity of SNNs, such models are still not feasible to train on real world tasks. These models therefore cannot demonstrate the implications of traveling waves on memory. In the machine learning community, [29] recently introduced the Neural Wave Machine, which exhibits traveling waves of activity in its hidden state in the service of sequence modeling; however, due to its construction as a network of coupled oscillators, it is impossible to disassociate the memory-enhancing contributions of oscillations (as described by [30]) from those of traveling waves.

In this work, we derive and introduce a simple non-oscillatory recurrent neural network (RNN) architecture which exhibits traveling waves in its hidden state, and we study the performance implications of these waves when compared directly with identical wave-free 'bump system' RNN counterparts. We find that wave-based models are able to solve sequence modeling tasks of significantly greater length, learn faster, and reach lower error than non-wave counterparts, approaching the performance of more complicated state of the art architectures, thereby providing some of the first computational evidence for the benefits of wave-based memory systems. We therefore present our model both as a proof of concept of the computational role of wave-based memory systems and as a starting point for the continued development of such systems in the future.
